extracted.intended_audience: novelists, creative-writing students, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and handling point of view and on 'dramatizing' a character's consciousness so that undramatic subjects gain dramatic force through showing surface images and scenes rather than authorial exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reach the subject through a character's consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject can only be reached through Strether’s consciousness; that way alone will command the impression that the scene makes on him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present the story, impressions, and setting as filtered through a central character's perception rather than as independent facts; render people, places, and the 'picture' (e.g., Paris in spring) as that character's vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit authorial intrusion into the point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: To see it, even for a moment, from some different angle—if, for example, the author interposed with a vision of his own—would patently disturb the right impression. The author does no such thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the author's voice unobtrusive; avoid inserting a separate authoritative vision that would contradict or reframe the chosen point of view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize thought by showing its surface images
rubrics_metrics.description: When it is time to learn what he makes of it...we must see for ourselves, the author must so arrange matters that Strether’s thought will all be made intelligible by a direct view of its surface. The immediate flaw or ripple of the moment, and the next and the next, will then take up the tale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render inner life as a sequence of visible, transient mental images, gestures, and ripples rather than by retrospective summary or abstract exposition; let those surface moments 'act' the thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid explanatory exposition of a character's inner substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose him to begin sharing the knowledge that he alone possesses...he must at once give us the whole of it, must let us into every secret without delay, or his exposition is plainly misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not have a character or narrator fall into full explanatory disclosure of inner motives after the fact; once exposition begins the reader assumes total disclosure, which undermines suspense and dramatization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use staged, incremental glimpses to portray change
rubrics_metrics.description: To bring his mind into view at the different moments, one after another, when it is brushed by new experience—to multiply these glimpses until the silent change is apparent, though no word has actually been said of it: this is Henry James’s way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show internal change as an accumulation of small scenes and moments rather than by announcing a turning point; use repeated, varied surface instances to make a private transformation visible to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain dramatic privileges even where summary seems appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: He arrives at the point where apparently nothing but a summary and a report should be possible, and even there he is precluded from none of the privileges of a dramatist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even passages that might conventionally be summarized can be treated dramatically by arranging moments and speech to enact the change rather than merely narrating it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let dialogue and description be continuous in method
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything in the novel is now dramatically rendered, whether it is a page of dialogue or a page of description...When the story passes from these to the scenes of dialogue...there is thus no break in the method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the same 'dramatic' technique across both descriptive passages and exchanges of speech so the POV remains seamless and the reader's experience is consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the reader an active interpreter of the point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: The point of view is itself a matter for the reader to confront and to watch constructively...that point of view shall appeal directly to the onlooker, and not by way of any summarizing picture-maker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the narrative so readers must infer, assemble, and judge the character's mind from presented moments rather than relying on an explicit narrator to interpret events for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let a first-person narrator invalidate suspense in some genres
rubrics_metrics.description: In a tale of murder and mystery there is one man who cannot possibly be the narrator, and that is the murderer himself; for if he admits us into his mind at all he must do so without reserve, thereby betraying the secret that we ought to be guessing at for ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of genre constraints: certain narratorial positions (e.g., murderer-as-narrator) can logically eliminate mystery; choose POV to preserve necessary ignorance and suspense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scenes to replace expository 'harking back'
rubrics_metrics.description: He himself...calls attention to the way in which a conversation...puts the reader in possession of all the past facts of the situation which it is necessary for him to know; a scene thus takes the place of that 'harking back to make up.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide background and exposition organically through scenes and dialogue rather than through lumps of retrospective narrative; let scenes reveal needed facts in the present action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat undramatic subjects by animating descriptive elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The less dramatic, strictly speaking, the subject may be...the more it is needful to heighten its flat, pictorial, descriptive surface by the arts of drama...The dramatic rule is applied more fundamentally; it animates the actual elements of the picture, the description, and makes a drama of these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When subject matter lacks overt action, render its description with the energy and structure of drama—use gestures, images, and staged moments to create dramatic effect rather than inserting pointless dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid peppering scenes with idle animated dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not managed by peppering the surface with animated dialogue, by making the characters break into talk when they really have nothing to contribute to the subject; the end of this is only to cheapen and discredit their talk when at length it is absolutely required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only include spoken exchanges that materially contribute to the dramatic or cognitive effect; avoid putting characters onstage to deliver empty talk merely to add 'animation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use selective, indirect revelation to give solidity to hidden facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Not to walk straight up to the fact and put it into phrases, but to surround the fact, and so to detach it inviolate—such is Henry James’s manner of dramatizing it...the enlightening word did not seem peculiarly emphatic as it was uttered, it was not announced with any particular circumstance; and yet, presently—there was the piece of knowledge that I had not possessed before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reveal crucial information by surrounding it with indirect cues, glances, and seemingly incidental moments so that the reader experiences recognition rather than being bluntly told.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the surface manifestations imply deeper realities
rubrics_metrics.description: The superficial play of thought...is all we actually see; for the most part it is very light...And yet, presently—these are the troubles that engage her in solitude...Not by direct allusion but by skirting round them, giving one brief sight of her in eloquent circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey inner conflicts through small, surface-level disturbances—expressions, pauses, attitudes—so that readers infer the deeper situation from outward signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ economy: choose whether a narrator adds value
rubrics_metrics.description: I take it as evident that unless the presence of a seer and a recorder is made a value in itself, contributing definitely to the effect of the subject, he is better dispensed with and put out of the way...the narrator...represents the great principle of economy, and is a value in himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide deliberately whether a narrator's interpretive presence enhances the story; if not, remove or minimize that presence and allow direct presentation to stand on its own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve dramatic detachment during scenic dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply it consists in treating the scene as dramatically as possible—keeping it framed in Strether’s vision, certainly, but keeping his consciousness out of sight, his thought unexplored...to us, to the reader, his voice seems as much as hers to belong to somebody whom we are watching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During scenes, present characters' speech and behavior so the reader can observe them as if from outside the character's mind—retain the POV framing but avoid internal commentary that collapses the scene's objectivity.
